proposed_edges.relationship: In Herman Paul’s 2019 assessment, White’s work became philosophy of history’s shared reference point, built on by Harlan, Kleinberg and Kuukkanen and contested by others; White himself assigned philosophy of history to the “practical past” (2010)
proposed_edges.map_label: Paul: White as the field’s reference point, 2019
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Paul's author manuscript, read in full (Journal of the Philosophy of History 13, 2019; manuscript pages): "no other author occupies a position in the field that is remotely as central as White’s" (ms 1); his only measure is his own JSTOR count of History and Theory articles mentioning White (ms 10 n. 22), with Harlan, Kleinberg and Kuukkanen positioning themselves towards him (ms 10–11). White's own words, read in full (Historein 10, 2010, p. 18): "philosophy of history belongs to the class of disciplines meant to bring order and reason to a 'practical past'". Counterweight: Timmins (Reviews in History, 2011) remains "to be convinced that White's impact on historical writing is as great as the current narratives claim" — a claim about historians' practice, not philosophy of history. Reciprocal to edge_166 (the earlier philosophers White engaged), not parallel to it.

proposed_edges.relationship: Philosophers of history contest White’s narrativism, as Herman Paul reports: Ricoeur on the constraints set by sources, David Carr on narrative in lived experience, Lorenz’s internal realism, Ankersmit on untheorised tropes and Runia on presence (1985–2013)
proposed_edges.map_label: Ricoeur, David Carr, Lorenz, Ankersmit, Runia, per Paul
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated: the critics' texts are unread and known through Paul's manuscript, read in full (2019, ms 17–19): Ankersmit finds the tropology "not nearly philosophical enough"; for Ricoeur sources "set constraints" and White "runs a risk of erasing genre boundaries between history and fiction" (Temps et récit 3, 1985); David Carr (1986); "'internal realists' such as Chris Lorenz argue that White downplays the importance of rational debate among historians"; Runia's "presence" against "Whitean representationalism" (2006). Paul's caveat: criticism is sometimes "a response elicited by the perceived dominance of his work" (ms 19). A second witness for David Carr: Cronon (1992, pp. 1368–1369, read) prefers Carr's position to White's and Mink's. Distinct from edge_257, where historians (Ginzburg, Evans) answer postmodernism.

proposed_edges.relationship: A historian of European thought before Metahistory, who coauthored two textbooks on liberal humanism in Western Europe (1966, 1970) and wrote essays on the tasks of intellectual history, as Paul and Sanz Loroño report; Martin Jay ranks his reflections on the craft with Skinner’s (2013)
proposed_edges.map_label: Intellectual historian of Europe, per readers
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated: the 1960s books and essays are unread. Paul (2019, ms 13 n. 32, read in full): The Emergence of Liberal Humanism: An Intellectual History of Western Europe (1966, with Coates and Schapiro) and The Ordeal of Liberal Humanism (1970, with Coates). Sanz Loroño (Historiografías, 2011, p. 143, read in full): The Fiction of Narrative reprints "The tasks of intellectual history" and "Romanticism, historicism, and realism", the latter readable "como un Metahistory anterior al impacto del (pos) estructuralismo francés". Stovall's AHA memorial (2018, WebFetch) presents him as an intellectual historian and theorist. Jay (History and Theory, 2013, abstract only): "No contemporary intellectual historian has produced more influential reflections on the historian's craft than Hayden White and Quentin Skinner". No strand is targeted.

proposed_edges.relationship: White asks what limits govern the stories that can responsibly be told about the Holocaust (Probing the Limits of Representation, 1992; reprinted in Figural Realism); the quoted excerpt makes a conditional argument about facts determining plots. His 2014 contents also list “Truth and Circumstance …”; that chapter is unread
proposed_edges.evidence_note: An excerpt witness: the passages of the essay quoted by Claus and Marriott, whose framing is theirs (white_emplotment_excerpt, existing reading, re-read for revision 1.147): "Are there any limits on the kind of story that can responsibly be told about these phenomena?"; facts set limits on stories "only if we believe that the events themselves possess a 'story' kind of form and a 'plot' kind of meaning" — a conditional argument about facts determining plots, not a claim that all emplotments are equally valid, and not the full argument of the chapter. The essay's pages (37–53 in Friedländer's volume) and its discussion by Ginzburg and Funkenstein come from Domańska's bibliography; MUSE contents show it reprinted as Figural Realism ch. 2 (pp. 27–42) and the 2014 chapter "Truth and Circumstance: What (if Anything) Can Properly Be Said about the Holocaust?" (pp. 25–40), both unread. Paul (2019, ms 15) records his later "forays into 'modernist events,' … witness literature, trauma". Holocaust representation was previously carried only at group level (edges 223, 224) and in Friedländer's roster row.

proposed_edges.relationship: Cronon builds on White’s distinction between chronicle and narrative, then sides with David Carr against the White–Mink view that historians impose plots on reality (1992)
proposed_edges.map_label: Chronicle and narrative: used and contested, 1992
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cronon's own text, read in part for this edge ("A Place for Stories", JAH 78:4, 1992, author-hosted copy in journal pagination): p. 1351 n. 7, "This distinction between chronicle and narrative is more fully analyzed in White, Metahistory, 5-7; White, Tropics of Discourse, 109-11"; p. 1368, White and Mink "argue that narrative is so basic to our cultural beliefs that we automatically impose it on a reality that bears little or no relation to the plots we use" (Cronon's summary of their position); n. 39 calls White's 1984 survey "useful, if biased"; pp. 1368–1369, Carr's position "gives us a way of absorbing the lessons of narrative theory without feeling we have abandoned all ties to an external reality". One essay makes both moves, so one arrow records an acknowledged and contested resource (the pattern of edge_646). edge_903 (Cronon → truthdebate) uses other pages of the same essay for his own position.

new_sources.title: Herman Paul, “A Loosely Knit Network: Philosophy of History After Hayden White,” Journal of the Philosophy of History 13 (2019): 3–20.
new_sources.citation: Herman Paul, “A Loosely Knit Network: Philosophy of History After Hayden White,” Journal of the Philosophy of History 13 (2019): 3–20.

verification.note: Author's manuscript in the Leiden University repository (https://hdl.handle.net/1887/69888) read in full for revision 1.147 (21 manuscript pages with notes); pages cited are manuscript pages, not journal pages. ms 1: White's death in March 2018; "no other author occupies a position in the field that is remotely as central as White’s … philosophers of history relate to White’s work, either by building upon it or by dissociating themselves from it." ms 10–11 and n. 22: a JSTOR search of History and Theory 1960–2013 "yields 428 hits for 'Hayden White' and 142 hits for 'Hayden V. White'" (Paul's count of articles mentioning him); Harlan, Kleinberg and Kuukkanen position themselves towards White. ms 13 n. 32: the textbooks The Emergence of Liberal Humanism (1966, with Coates and Schapiro) and The Ordeal of Liberal Humanism (1970, with Coates). ms 14: "Metahistory did not intend to replace 'explanation' by 'narrative.' Instead, the book argued that historians explain, among other things, through narrative means." ms 15–16: The Content of the Form; later forays into "'modernist events,' 'intransitive writing,' witness literature, trauma, the sublime, and the 'practical past'". ms 17–19: criticism "from all sides": Ankersmit (tropology "not nearly philosophical enough"), Ricoeur (sources "set constraints"; White "runs a risk of erasing genre boundaries between history and fiction"), David Carr (1986), "'internal realists' such as Chris Lorenz" who argue that "White downplays the importance of rational debate among historians", Runia's "presence" against "Whitean representationalism"; criticism is sometimes "a response elicited by the perceived dominance of his work" (ms 19). The centrality claim is Paul's.

Open access (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); read in full for revision 1.147, printed pp. 10–19 (the cover sheet's "2011" and "© 2012" are posting dates; volume 10 is dated 2010). p. 14: Kant's practical question "what should I (we) do?" leads to "the practical past". p. 16: "The practical past is made up of all those memories, illusions, bits of vagrant information, attitudes and values which the individual or the group summons up as best they can to justify, dignify, excuse, alibi or make a case for actions to be taken in the prosecution of a life project"; after Oakeshott (n. 3) and Koselleck's "space of experience" (n. 2); "the historical past was a past constructed by historians. It existed in books and scholarly essays only." p. 17: professional historiography was set up in the universities "to serve the interests of the nation-state". p. 18: "philosophy of history belongs to the class of disciplines meant to bring order and reason to a 'practical past' rather than to that 'historical past' constructed by professional historians".

new_sources.title: Gabrielle M. Spiegel, “Hayden White’s Return to the Past as a Source of Human Practice,” Práticas da História 6 (2018): 127–135.
new_sources.citation: Gabrielle M. Spiegel, “Hayden White’s Return to the Past as a Source of Human Practice,” Práticas da História 6 (2018): 127–135.

verification.note: Open-access journal PDF read in full for revision 1.147, pp. 127–135. White used "the concept of the practical past, borrowed from Michael Oakeshott, as a means to argue for individual choices --ethical, moral and existential-- in contemporary life, and hence as a way to escape the burden of history" (abstract, p. 127); "if one considers 'The Burden of History' and 'The Practical Past' as the framing articles of White’s career, then Metahistory … can be seen as the instrument chosen by White to liberate humankind from the tyranny of the (positivist) past" (pp. 129–130). Mediated quotations: The Practical Past (2014), preface xiii and pp. 8–9, 12–15; White's 2005 reply to Moses, p. 336: history "has sold out any claim to relevance to present existential concerns of the societies in which it is practiced in order to purchase a much more dubious claim to 'objectivity' in the study of the past" (Spiegel, p. 132). An admirer's reception statement.

pe131_cronon_place_stories_1992.note: Revision 1.147 (Hayden White edges) newly read pp. 1350–1351 and 1368–1369 in journal pagination, so p. 1368 is no longer among the pages not read closely. p. 1350 n. 6: reading list naming White's Metahistory (1973), Tropics of Discourse (1978) and The Content of the Form (1987). p. 1351 and n. 7: Great Plains history as "a chronicle, a simple chronological listing of events"; "This distinction between chronicle and narrative is more fully analyzed in White, Metahistory, 5-7; White, Tropics of Discourse, 109-11; Louis O. Mink". p. 1368: "One group, which includes Hayden White and the late Louis Mink as well as many of the deconstructionists, argues that narrative is so basic to our cultural beliefs that we automatically impose it on a reality that bears little or no relation to the plots we use in organizing our experience" (Cronon's summary of their position); n. 39 calls White's 1984 History and Theory survey "useful, if biased". pp. 1368–1369: the alternative "most recently defended by David Carr"; "Carr's position will undoubtedly be attractive to most historians" and "gives us a way of absorbing the lessons of narrative theory without feeling we have abandoned all ties to an external reality."
